Fixing the MoE GEMM pipeline and batching tile sweeps
Memory summary

The agent found that a three-stage cp.async pipeline read unwritten shared memory, producing NaNs at T=1. It corrected the producer and consumer slot indexing in both GEMMs, reduced padded warp work, and built a single-module tile sweep to limit time spent waiting for the contended GPU lock. The unit ended with Python syntax and CUDA-language checks passing; correctness and performance results were still pending.

Relevant prior context

The GPU’s measured read bandwidth was 1541.5 GB/s under best-of-30 probing; earlier lower readings were attributed to concurrent GPU jobs. The design depended on keeping repeated GEMM panels in L2.

Important non-obvious context

The target was an SM120 RTX PRO 6000 with CUDA 13.0. The measured dynamic shared-memory opt-in limit was 99 KiB per CTA. The GPU lock serialized jobs only within the benchmark; other processes could still use the GPU, and this run spent substantial time queued behind another job.

The sweep harness and debug scripts were development aids. They did not change the required Model interface or routed/shared parameter names used to load the reference state dict. No correctness result, benchmark score, or winner configuration was established in this unit.

Recording summary

1. Tightened the existing kernels while the first check ran. The agent changed the inline BF16 MMA helper to accumulate in place using "+f" operands, avoiding a separate materialized C accumulator. It rewrote shared-memory copy loops with compile-time trip counts and #pragma unroll, and added warp-uniform skips for warps whose rows were entirely padding. Inactive warps still participated in async copies and barriers.

2. Diagnosed and fixed the NaNs. The check exposed systematic NaNs at T=1. The prologue filled stages 0 and 1 of a three-slot pipeline, but the loop later read stage 2. The refill path also targeted the slot just consumed instead of the earlier-drained slot. The agent’s diagnosis was:

``text The prologue loads stages 0..STAGES-2 (0 and 1), leaving stage 2 empty. But the loop computes from stage = kb % STAGES, so at kb=2 it reads stage 2 — never written. The in-loop load also writes back into the slot it just consumed (kb%3) instead of the correct slot for chunk kb+STAGES-1, which is (kb+STAGES-1)%STAGES. Garbage bf16 → inf accumulators → inf * up = NaN. ``

Both GEMMs were updated to track separate stage and fill indices. The prologue initializes the first STAGES-1 chunks; each iteration consumes stage, refills fill with chunk kb+STAGES-1, then advances both indices. The dynamic shared-memory declaration was also explicitly aligned to 16 bytes.

3. Prepared diagnostics and reduced harness memory use. The agent planned to expose the permuted intermediate and routing arrays to isolate failures by stage. It also split timing-only model construction from reference-model construction because each model held 12.9 GB of weights. A profiling driver was added to measure DRAM reads and L2 hit rate, testing the assumption that each expert’s weights would be fetched from DRAM once.

4. Batched the tile sweep to cope with queueing. The correctness/timing run waited behind another job, so the agent changed the launcher to compile several tile configurations into one module and dispatch at runtime. The initial configurations varied BM, BK, pipeline depth, and warp layout; a later BM=256 configuration aimed to keep each expert to one m-tile at T=4096. The agent noted that BM=256 with a larger gate/up tile would exceed the register budget.

Static checks reported all six initial configurations under the 99 KiB shared-memory cap and within the listed division and accumulator-register constraints. For the added configuration, the reported estimate was:

``text cfg6: thr 512/512 smem 72K/72K gemm1 acc=64 frag=24 est=108 cap=128 OK gemm2 acc=64 frag=24 est=108 cap=128 OK divis 0000 ``

The unified module exposed a development-only config selector and num_cfgs(). The combined harness was set to compare configurations against cfg0, then time all configurations over the benchmark shapes. Since the earlier correctness result had not arrived, cross-configuration agreement was only a planned check, not proof of correctness.

5. Canceled the queued partial run and launched one combined run. The agent observed that a queued run had waited more than 25 minutes, killed that single-purpose queued run, and submitted correctness followed by the full configuration sweep under one lock acquisition. The combined run remained pending at the unit boundary.

6. Verified syntax and CUDA-language eligibility. Python compilation succeeded, and the environment reported:

``text forbidden hits: NONE cuda_language ok: True framework: ptx evidence: ['global_kernel', 'cuda_header', 'ptx_inline'] ``

No benchmark timing or official peak_fraction score was reported in this unit.

GLM-5.2 fused MoE on RTX PRO 6000 — official score 0.0653
Memory summary

The solution implements routing, gate/up projection with fused SiLU multiplication, down projection, weighted accumulation, and bf16 conversion in a load_inline CUDA/PTX extension. The official run passed correctness and the CUDA-language check, received a clean audit verdict, and scored 0.0653: rank 17 among 19 scored leaderboard entries.

Relevant prior context

The target was an SM120 RTX PRO 6000. During setup, GPU utilization and three concurrent compute jobs explained unexpectedly inconsistent probe timings. A best-of-30 bandwidth probe measured 1541.5 GB/s, or 85.6% of the stated 1.8 TB/s bandwidth.

The implementation treats the 256 routed experts and shared expert as a grouped workload. Routing kernels count expert IDs, build offsets and tile descriptors, and scatter token IDs and weights into expert-sorted order. The shared expert occupies an extra expert slot, receives every token in identity order, and uses weight 1.0. Two grouped GEMMs use bf16 mma.sync with cp.async pipelining; the first computes gate and up together and fuses SiLU-times-up, while the second weights and scatters results into an fp32 output before bf16 conversion.

The source explains the tile-ordering rationale:

// grid.x = n-tile (fastest-varying) so consecutive CTAs share an A panel, and
// the m-tiles of one expert stay close enough to share their B panel in L2.

Development found and fixed a cp.async pipeline-slot bug involving uninitialized shared memory. The final source leaves tile configuration 0 as the default; it uses BM=128, a 64-column first-GEMM tile, a 128-column second-GEMM tile, and three pipeline stages.

Important non-obvious context

The benchmark is compute-regime graded against a stated bf16 peak of 500 TFLOPS, but several shapes perform poorly, especially short batches. Official per-shape results were:

The official score is the geometric mean of those peak fractions. The leaderboard had 20 cells, 19 scored entries, and a best score of 0.113.

The CUDA-language gate labeled the implementation ptx; the audit confirms this is an accepted CUDA/PTX category. It reported ok=true, CUDA evidence, and no forbidden-operation hits. The audit also found the numeric stress suite passed at the deck’s bf16 tolerance of 0.08. It found no grader mutation, tolerance changes, output caching, graph replay, or cross-run artifact reuse; template files matched the live deck.

Recording summary

The final source uses torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline, CUDA runtime and bf16 headers, and inline PTX for cp.async, ldmatrix, and mma.sync. It defines the expected parameter names and shapes so the checker can load the reference state dict. Each call allocates fresh routing metadata, intermediate activations, and output accumulators.
